summary: Carbocisteine (carbocysteine) is a mucolytic / mucoregulating agent used to reduce the viscosity of bronchial secretions and facilitate expectoration in conditions associated with excessive or viscid mucus, such as chronic bronchitis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. It is NOT approved by the US FDA but is widely licensed in the UK, Europe, and Asia, so this information is based on the Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC) and BNF. Unlike acetylcysteine it does not contain a free thiol group; instead it acts intracellularly on goblet cells to normalise the proportion of sialomucins and fucomucins, restoring more normal mucus rheology. The usual adult dose is 750 mg three times daily initially, reduced to 750 mg twice daily (1.5 g/day) once a satisfactory response is obtained. It is contraindicated in active peptic ulceration (it may disrupt the gastric mucosal barrier). It is generally well tolerated; gastrointestinal upset is the most common side effect, and severe skin reactions have rarely been reported.
indications: Reduction of mucus viscosity to aid expectoration in disorders associated with excessive, viscous mucus (e.g. chronic bronchitis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease)

moa: Carbocisteine is a mucoactive agent that acts within bronchial goblet cells to influence the synthesis of mucus. It normalises the abnormal ratio of sialomucins to fucomucins seen in hypersecretory airway disease, reducing the viscosity and elasticity of the mucus and making it easier to clear by ciliary action and coughing. Unlike acetylcysteine, carbocisteine lacks a free sulfhydryl (thiol) group and does not act by breaking disulfide bonds in mucus extracellularly; instead it has an intracellular mucoregulatory action. Some antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects on the airway mucosa have also been described.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to carbocisteine or any component of the formulation
relative: Pregnancy (particularly first trimester) and lactation - avoid unless essential
Patients who cannot clear increased secretions (e.g. very weak cough)

preg: There are limited data on carbocisteine use in pregnancy. As a precaution it should be avoided during pregnancy, especially the first trimester, unless considered essential by the prescriber.
lact: There is limited information on whether carbocisteine is excreted in breast milk. As a precaution, avoid use during breastfeeding unless considered essential.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is required for renal impairment in standard labelling; use with usual clinical caution.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment is required for hepatic impairment in standard labelling; use with general caution.

counsel: This medicine thins phlegm so it is easier to cough up - take it as prescribed

pearls: Carbocisteine is NOT FDA-approved - this record reflects the EU/UK SmPC and BNF; confirm local labelling before use.
It is a mucoregulator that works intracellularly (no free thiol group), distinguishing it from acetylcysteine.
Contraindicated in active peptic ulceration because it can disrupt the gastric mucus barrier.
Do not co-prescribe with antitussives or antimuscarinic drying agents - they oppose its purpose.
Generally well tolerated; rare severe skin reactions (SJS/TEN) warrant prompt discontinuation if a serious rash appears.
Reduce to the maintenance dose (1.5 g/day) once a clinical response is achieved.
missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your normal schedule - do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose is expected mainly to cause gastrointestinal effects such as nausea, gastric irritation, and diarrhoea. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive and symptomatic, with attention to hydration and gastrointestinal symptoms; gastric decontamination is rarely needed given the low toxicity.
